meta.description: A self-hosting handbook: the fundamentals, a setup path in eight stages and Compose templates tailored to your domain, paths and reverse proxy.
lang.name: English
lang.hint: This page is also available in English.
banner.label: Work in progress
banner.text: yourhomelab isn't finished yet. Many guides are still missing, and templates may change.
home.title: Your own server. Step by step.
home.lead: yourhomelab explains the fundamentals, walks you through the setup in eight stages and provides Compose files for the services you want to run. Tailored to your domain, your paths and your reverse proxy.
home.door1.title: Understand
home.door1.text: Concepts and background, organized like a wiki. For when you want to know why something works the way it does.
home.door2.title: Build
home.door2.text: Eight stages from an empty machine to a running homelab. You can tick off every step.
home.door3.title: Run
home.door3.text: Compose files for {n} services that adapt to your domain, paths and reverse proxy.
home.homelabsLead: How do others run theirs? From a single mini PC to a cluster: browse real setups and show your own.
home.faqLead: What yourhomelab is, what it isn't, and where else to find help.
home.decideText: Three questions about your internet connection, your data and your hardware. Afterwards you'll know where your server should live.
home.contributeText: All guides and Compose templates are openly available in the repository. Found a mistake or missing a service? Send a pull request or open an issue.
home.supportText: yourhomelab is free and ad-free. If a guide saved you time, the project appreciates a small donation.
oneway.title: One way among many
oneway.text: yourhomelab describes one possible setup: specific tools, conventions and directory structures. There are many other good ways, and you can shape your setup differently at any time. Guides and templates do build on each other, though, and work best if you stick to the conventions described here.
wiki.title: Learn
wiki.lead: Concepts and background on self-hosting. Pick a topic from the list or start with the fundamentals.
wiki.notYetText: We don't cover Kubernetes, k3s, Docker Swarm, Ansible and Terraform yet. Everything here builds on one server running Docker Compose.
page.stubText: The page exists, the content doesn't yet. Know your way around this topic? Write it directly on GitHub, the file is already there.
page.untranslated: This page hasn't been translated yet. You're seeing the original German version.
setup.title: Set up
setup.lead: Eight stages from an empty machine to a running homelab. The stages build on each other, and you can tick off every guide.
services.title: Services
services.lead: Every service comes with a tested compose.yaml and .env. The files adapt to your setup before you copy them.
services.missingText: Suggest it on GitHub or submit a template directly as a pull request.
homelabs.title: Homelabs
homelabs.lead: How other people run their homelab, from a single mini PC to a Kubernetes cluster. Every setup is one way among many, and none of them is the one right way.
homelabs.exampleNote: This entry is an example by yourhomelab, not a real person's homelab.
homelabs.submitText: Fill in the form on GitHub and we'll turn it into an entry. It doesn't matter how big or small your setup is.
tools.title: Tools
tools.lead: Small helpers for getting started and running your homelab. They build on your "My setup" and run entirely in your browser.
tools.privacy: Everything you enter here stays in your browser. Nothing is sent to a server.
tools.assistant.title: Getting-started assistant
tools.assistant.desc: A few questions about your hardware, connection and preferences. At the end you get a recommended path, and "My setup" is set up to match.
tools.stack-builder.title: Stack builder
tools.stack-builder.desc: Pick your services and download everything as one package: folders, compose.yaml, .env with ready-made secrets and a script to start them.
tools.compose-explainer.title: Compose explainer
tools.compose-explainer.desc: Paste any compose.yaml. Every line gets explained and common problems are flagged.
tools.proxy-config.title: Proxy config
tools.proxy-config.desc: Traefik labels, a Caddyfile entry or Nginx Proxy Manager values for a service that isn't in the catalog.
tools.password-hash.title: Secrets & password hash
tools.password-hash.desc: Creates random secrets of any length for your .env and bcrypt hashes for Tinyauth and basic auth. Everything happens in your browser.
tools.borgmatic.title: borgmatic config
tools.borgmatic.desc: Generates a borgmatic config.yaml from your setup and services, including database dumps and retention rules.
tools.docs-export.title: Docs export
tools.docs-export.desc: Turns your setup and services into a Markdown file with ports, paths and restore steps.
tools.security-check.title: Security check
tools.security-check.desc: A checklist for your homelab. At the end you see where you're in good shape and what's still missing.
tools.power-calculator.title: Power calculator
tools.power-calculator.desc: What does your server cost per year? Enter watts and your electricity price, done.
service.forcedSub: {name} only works on its own subdomain, so the template uses a subdomain instead of a path URL.
service.networkText: Only for your first service: create the shared proxy network. If it already exists, skip this command.
service.step2Text: Copy the files into the folder. Random values for passwords and keys are already filled into the .env, generated only in your browser.
service.step3Text: Docker pulls the images and starts all containers of the stack.
service.upstreamText: The project's official Compose file. It is not tailored to your setup.
service.contributeText: Mistake in the template or a new version? Improve it directly on GitHub.
proxy.caddy.desc: One entry per service in the Caddyfile
proxy.npm.desc: Proxy host in the web interface
proxy.none.desc: Publish ports directly on the server

tools.stack-builder.proxyMismatch: Your setup uses {setup}, and the files are prepared for it. If you want to use {name}, change it in “My setup”.

tools.stack-builder.downloadText: One folder per service with compose.yaml and .env, plus setup.sh and a README. All tailored to your setup.
tools.stack-builder.secretsNote: The passwords and keys in the .env files are generated randomly and exist only in this download. Keep the ZIP or the values somewhere safe, like your password manager.
tools.stack-builder.readme.title: Your homelab stack
tools.stack-builder.readme.intro: Created on {date} with the yourhomelab stack builder. Included: {services}.
tools.stack-builder.readme.step1: Copy the ZIP to your server, unpack it (`unzip homelab-stack.zip`) and change into the folder: `cd {folder}`.
tools.stack-builder.readme.step2: Look through the files: `compose.yaml` and `.env` in each subfolder. The passwords in the `.env` files are random. Keep them somewhere safe, like your password manager.
tools.stack-builder.readme.step3: Start everything with `bash setup.sh` (with `sudo` if needed). The script creates the folders under `{root}`, copies the files there and starts the containers. It never overwrites existing files.
tools.stack-builder.readme.step4: Add the entries from `PROXY.txt` to your reverse proxy.
tools.stack-builder.readme.more: Want to change something? Build a new package: {url}
tools.stack-builder.proxyFile.caddy:
Caddyfile blocks for your services.
Add them to {file} (the stack builder already put them there if Caddy is part of the package)
and reload Caddy: docker compose exec caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile

Proxy hosts for Nginx Proxy Manager.
In the web interface, go to Hosts → Proxy Hosts and add one entry per service with these values.

tools.compose-explainer.placeholder: Paste the contents of your compose.yaml here …
tools.compose-explainer.autoHint: The explanation updates as you type. Colored marks next to the line numbers show where to look.
tools.compose-explainer.empty: Paste a compose.yaml above or load the example. The explanation shows up here.
tools.compose-explainer.name: Project name
tools.compose-explainer.partial: As long as the file has syntax errors, the analysis below is incomplete.
tools.compose-explainer.jump: Jump to line {n} in the editor
tools.compose-explainer.err.TAB_AS_INDEN: This line is indented with a tab. YAML only allows spaces for indentation.
tools.compose-explainer.err.BAD_INDENT: The indentation is off. Entries on the same level must be indented exactly the same (2 spaces per level is common).
tools.compose-explainer.err.DUPLICATE_KE: A key appears twice on the same level. Remove one or merge them.
tools.compose-explainer.err.MISSING_CHAR: A character is missing here, often a closing quote or bracket.
tools.compose-explainer.err.BLOCK_AS_IMP: A nested structure starts where YAML doesn’t expect one. Usually a space after the colon is missing or the indentation is off.
tools.compose-explainer.err.MULTILINE_IM: A key spans several lines. Often a colon or the space after it is missing, or a quote isn’t closed.
tools.compose-explainer.err.UNEXPECTED_T: YAML doesn’t expect this character here. Often it’s a colon without a space after it or a `-` in the wrong place.
tools.compose-explainer.err.BAD_SCALAR_S: This value starts with a special character (such as `@`, `%` or a backtick). Put it in quotes.
tools.compose-explainer.err.BAD_DQ_ESCAP: Invalid escape sequence in double quotes. Use single quotes or double the backslash.
tools.compose-explainer.err.BAD_ALIAS: This refers to an anchor (`*name`) that doesn’t exist.
tools.compose-explainer.err.MULTIPLE_DOC: The file contains several YAML documents (`---`). Compose expects exactly one.
tools.compose-explainer.err.BLOCK_IN_FLO: A multi-line block sits inside `[ ]` or `{ }`. That isn’t allowed.
tools.compose-explainer.s.notMap: The file isn’t a YAML mapping (`key: value`). A compose.yaml starts with keys like `services:`.
tools.compose-explainer.s.noServices: The `services:` section is missing. That’s where the containers are defined.
tools.compose-explainer.s.servicesNotMap: Under `services:`, each service needs a name followed by a colon, with its settings indented below.
tools.compose-explainer.s.serviceNotMap: Service `{name}` has no settings. Indent at least an `image:` line below it.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.hub: Registry: Docker Hub (`docker.io`), the default when no registry is given.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.registry: Registry: `{registry}`. The image comes from there instead of Docker Hub.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.official: Name: `{repo}`, an official image on Docker Hub (no publisher prefix).
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.repo: Name: `{repo}`. The part before the `/` is usually the publisher (user or organization).
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.noTag: Tag: none given, so Docker uses `latest`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.latest: Tag: `latest`. Points to whatever the publisher tagged last and changes without you doing anything.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.floating: Tag: `{tag}`. A tag without a version number that can point to a different version after each release.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.major: Tag: `{tag}`, major version only. You get minor and patch updates, but no jump to the next major version.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.minor: Tag: `{tag}`. Major and minor version are fixed; patch updates (bug fixes) come in automatically.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.tag: Tag: `{tag}`, a fixed version. It only changes when you change the tag.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.digest: Digest: `{digest}`. The image is pinned to one exact build, even if the tag gets reassigned.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.db: This is a database. The major version matters a lot here because the data files are tied to it.
tools.compose-explainer.n.image.var: The image contains a variable. The final name comes from your `.env` or the shell.
tools.compose-explainer.n.container_name: Fixed container name `{value}`, handy for `docker logs {value}`. Without it, the container is called `<project>-<service>-1`. The name must be unique on the whole server.
tools.compose-explainer.n.restart.no: No automatic restart. After a crash or reboot, the container stays down.
tools.compose-explainer.n.restart.always: Always restarts, including after a reboot, even if you stopped it on purpose before.
tools.compose-explainer.n.restart.unless: Restarts after crashes and reboots unless you stopped it yourself. The usual choice for a homelab.
tools.compose-explainer.n.restart.on-fai: Only restarts when the process exits with an error.
tools.compose-explainer.n.port.map: Port `{host}` on the server forwards to port `{container}` in the container ({proto}). The server is always on the left, the container on the right.
tools.compose-explainer.n.port.container: Container port `{container}` only. Docker picks a random free port on the server for it.
tools.compose-explainer.n.port.all: Bound to all network interfaces: reachable by anyone who can reach the server (on your LAN, and from the internet with port forwarding).
tools.compose-explainer.n.port.local: Bound to `{ip}` only: reachable from the server itself (for example through an SSH tunnel), not from the network.
tools.compose-explainer.n.port.ip: Bound to `{ip}` only, so it’s reachable through that interface alone.
tools.compose-explainer.n.expose: Declares a port for other containers only. Nothing is published on the server.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.bind: Bind mount: `{source}` on the server shows up in the container at `{target}`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.relative: Bind mount relative to the compose.yaml folder: `{source}` shows up in the container at `{target}`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.named: Named volume `{source}`: Docker manages where it lives (under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`). Mounted at `{target}` in the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.anon: Anonymous volume for `{target}`: Docker creates a volume with a random name.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.tmpfs: tmpfs: `{target}` lives in memory only and is empty after a restart.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.ro: `:ro` means read-only: the container can read here, but not write.
tools.compose-explainer.n.vol.var: The path contains a variable. The real path comes from `.env`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.env.value: `{name}` gets a fixed value right from this file.
tools.compose-explainer.n.env.ref: `{name}` gets its value from the variable `{refs}`. Compose reads it from the `.env` next to compose.yaml or from your shell.
tools.compose-explainer.n.env.pass: `{name}` without a value: Compose passes through the variable of the same name from your shell. If it isn’t set there, the container doesn’t get it.
tools.compose-explainer.n.env_file: Every line of this file is loaded into the container as an environment variable.
tools.compose-explainer.n.net: The service joins the network `{name}`. Containers on the same network reach each other by service name.
tools.compose-explainer.n.net.external: External: this stack doesn’t create the network; it must already exist (for example the shared proxy network from `docker network create`).
tools.compose-explainer.n.network_mode.h: The container uses the server’s network directly. No isolation, `ports:` is ignored, and every port it opens is open on the server right away.
tools.compose-explainer.n.network_mode.s: Shares the network with `{value}`, typically to route traffic through a VPN container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.network_mode.n: No network: the container is fully offline.
tools.compose-explainer.n.dep.healthy: Waits until `{name}` is healthy according to its health check. The most reliable option.
tools.compose-explainer.n.dep.completed: Waits until `{name}` has finished successfully (for example a setup job).
tools.compose-explainer.n.label: Label `{key}`: a note attached to the container that other programs can read.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.enable: Tells Traefik to expose this container (needed when Traefik runs with `exposedByDefault=false`).
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.rule: Router `{router}`: requests for `{host}` go to this container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.rulePa: Router `{router}`: requests to the path `{path}` go to this container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.ruleOt: Router `{router}`: the rule that decides which requests end up here.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.entryp: Router `{router}` listens on the entrypoint `{value}` (on this site: `web` = port 80, `websecure` = port 443).
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.certre: Router `{router}` gets its TLS certificate automatically through the cert resolver `{value}` (Let’s Encrypt).
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.middle: Router `{router}` sends requests through `{value}` first (for example a login gate or headers).
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.servic: Router `{router}` forwards to the Traefik service `{value}`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.port: Traefik talks to the container internally on port `{value}`. No `ports:` needed for that.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.scheme: Traefik talks to the container over `{value}`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.middle: Defines the middleware `{name}` that routers can use.
tools.compose-explainer.n.traefik.networ: Traefik reaches the container through the network `{value}`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.healthcheck: Docker runs this command regularly (every {interval}) to check that the service actually works. You see the status in `docker ps`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.healthcheck.di: The health check built into the image is turned off.
tools.compose-explainer.n.user: The process runs as user/group `{value}` instead of root. New files in bind mounts belong to that ID.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap: An extra Linux privilege (capability) for the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.NET_ADMIN: Can change network settings (routes, firewall rules, VPN interfaces). Typical for VPN containers.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.NET_RAW: Can send raw network packets (for example for `ping`).
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.SYS_ADMIN: A very broad privilege (mounting file systems, among others). Close to root on the server.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.SYS_TIME: Can set the server’s system clock.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.SYS_MODULE: Can load kernel modules, which affects the whole server.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.SYS_PTRACE: Can inspect and manipulate other processes.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.ALL: All capabilities, practically the same as `privileged`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.CHOWN: Can change file ownership. Part of Docker’s default set anyway.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.SETUID: Can switch user IDs. Part of Docker’s default set anyway.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.SETGID: Can switch group IDs. Part of Docker’s default set anyway.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap.DAC_OVERRI: Can bypass file permissions. Part of Docker’s default set anyway.
tools.compose-explainer.n.cap_drop: Takes this privilege away from the container. Good for security.
tools.compose-explainer.n.privileged: The container gets almost all of the server’s privileges: every capability and access to all devices. Isolation is effectively gone.
tools.compose-explainer.n.pid.host: The container sees every process on the server.
tools.compose-explainer.n.devices: Passes the device `{dev}` into the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.devices.dri: Passes the GPU (`{dev}`) through, for example for hardware transcoding or machine learning.
tools.compose-explainer.n.devices.serial: Passes a serial device (`{dev}`) through, for example a Zigbee USB stick.
tools.compose-explainer.n.security_opt.n: `no-new-privileges`: processes in the container can’t gain extra privileges (for example through setuid programs).
tools.compose-explainer.n.security_opt: Security option for the container (for example AppArmor or seccomp).
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.build: Builds the image from a Dockerfile instead of pulling it.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.entrypoint: Overrides the program that runs at startup.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.extra_host: Extra entries in the container’s `/etc/hosts` (for example `host.docker.internal:host-gateway`).
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.logging: Settings for the container logs, such as a size limit.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.deploy: Resource limits and similar, such as a memory limit or a GPU reservation.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.tmpfs: Folders that live in memory only and are empty after every restart.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.init: Runs a tiny init process that forwards signals and reaps exited child processes.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.stop_grace: How long Docker waits on stop before killing the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.shm_size: Size of `/dev/shm` (shared memory). Some databases and browsers need more than the 64 MB default.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.secrets: Docker secrets: files with secret values, available in the container under `/run/secrets/`.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.configs: Config files that Compose places in the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.profiles: The service only starts when this profile is active (`docker compose --profile …`).
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.sysctls: Kernel parameters for this container only.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.ulimits: Limits, for example on the number of open files.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.dns: Custom DNS servers for the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.read_only: The container’s file system is read-only; only volumes are writable. Good for security.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.tty: Gives the container a terminal (like `docker run -t`).
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.pull_polic: Controls when Compose pulls the image again.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.group_add: Extra groups for the process, for example for device access.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.stop_signa: Signal used to stop the container.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.ipc: IPC mode (shared memory with other containers or the server).
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.x: Extension field (`x-…`): Compose ignores it. It’s usually a template for YAML anchors.
tools.compose-explainer.n.key.unknown: `{key}` isn’t explained in detail here. Check the Compose reference.
tools.compose-explainer.f.latest.why: With no tag or `latest`, every `docker compose pull` gets whatever is newest, including big jumps with breaking changes. You also can’t tell which version is running, and rolling back is hard.
tools.compose-explainer.f.latest.fix: Pin a version, such as `name:1.2.3`, or at least the major version (`name:1`). You’ll find the tags on the image’s registry page. Then you update on purpose by bumping the tag.
tools.compose-explainer.f.floatingTag.wh: Tags without a version number point to a different version after each release. Convenient, but updates arrive unplanned.
tools.compose-explainer.f.floatingTag.fi: If the image offers version tags, switch to a version number and apply updates on purpose.
tools.compose-explainer.f.pinned.why: You know exactly what’s running, and updates only happen when you want them.
tools.compose-explainer.f.dbMajor.t: `{service}`: database without a pinned major version (`{image}`)
tools.compose-explainer.f.dbMajor.why: A database’s data files only fit its major version. If the image jumps from, say, PostgreSQL 16 to 17, the database won’t start with the old data or needs an upgrade.
tools.compose-explainer.f.dbMajor.fix: Pin at least the major version, such as `postgres:16` or `mariadb:11.4`. If the database is already running, check the logs for the version it starts and pin exactly that. Plan major upgrades later on purpose (backup first, then upgrade).
tools.compose-explainer.f.publicPort.why: Docker writes published ports straight into the kernel’s firewall rules and bypasses UFW. So the port is open even if UFW doesn’t allow it: on your LAN, and on the internet with port forwarding.
tools.compose-explainer.f.publicPort.fix: If only the server itself needs access, bind to localhost: `"127.0.0.1:8080:80"`. If the service sits behind a reverse proxy, you usually don’t need `ports:` at all, because the proxy reaches it over the shared Docker network.
tools.compose-explainer.f.portsWithProxy: Traefik reaches the container over the Docker network. The extra published port is a second way in that skips Traefik: no HTTPS, no login gate, and Docker bypasses UFW.
Remove `ports:` (or bind to `127.0.0.1` for testing). Tell Traefik the internal port with the `loadbalancer.server.port` label.
tools.compose-explainer.f.localPort.why: The service is only reachable from the server itself, not from the network.
tools.compose-explainer.f.unquotedPort.w: Some YAML parsers read values like `22:22` as a base-60 number. That’s why the Docker docs recommend always quoting port mappings.
tools.compose-explainer.f.dockerSock.why: Whoever has the Docker socket can start any container, including one that mounts the whole server file system as root. Socket access is equivalent to root on the server. `:ro` barely helps: it only protects the socket file, not the commands sent through it.
tools.compose-explainer.f.dockerSock.fix: Only give the socket to tools you really trust (such as Traefik or Portainer). Better: put a socket proxy in between that allows read-only calls, and don’t expose the service directly to the internet.
tools.compose-explainer.f.plainSecret.t: `{service}`: `{name}` is in plain text in the file
tools.compose-explainer.f.plainSecret.wh: A compose.yaml easily ends up in Git, in screenshots or forum posts. Any password in it is then public.
tools.compose-explainer.f.plainSecret.fi: Move the value into the `.env` next to compose.yaml and write `{ref}` here. Keep `.env` out of public Git repos. If the file has already been shared, change the password.
tools.compose-explainer.f.secretRef.why: The values aren’t in compose.yaml, so you can share it or keep it in Git safely.
tools.compose-explainer.f.noRestart.why: Without `restart`, the container stays down after a crash or a server reboot.
tools.compose-explainer.f.restartSet.t: All services have a restart policy
tools.compose-explainer.f.restartSet.why: After a reboot, the stack comes back up on its own.
tools.compose-explainer.f.namedVolume.wh: Named volumes live under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`, not in your homelab folder. If you only back up that folder, they’re missing from the backup, and they’re easy to forget when you move.
tools.compose-explainer.f.namedVolume.fi: Use a bind mount into the stack folder instead, such as `./data:{target}`. Or add the volume to your backup explicitly.
tools.compose-explainer.f.anonVolume.why: Docker creates a volume with a random name for it. It’s gone quickly when you clean up, and it isn’t in your backup.
tools.compose-explainer.f.anonVolume.fix: Give the path a fixed place, such as `./data:{target}`.
tools.compose-explainer.f.undeclaredVolu: A named volume must be listed under the top-level `volumes:`, or Compose stops with an error. Or did you mean a folder? Then it needs `./` in front.
Add a top-level `volumes:` with `{volume}:` below it, or write `./{volume}` if it should be a folder next to compose.yaml.
tools.compose-explainer.f.undeclaredNetw: Every network a service uses must be listed under the top-level `networks:`. Otherwise the stack won’t start.
Add a top-level `networks:` with `{network}:` below it. For a network that already exists (like the proxy network), also set `external: true`.
tools.compose-explainer.f.unknownDep.why: Compose can only wait for services in the same file and stops otherwise.
tools.compose-explainer.f.unknownDep.fix: Check the spelling. The name must match a service under `services:` exactly.
tools.compose-explainer.f.homePath.why: Data in your home folder ends up scattered and isn’t included when you back up the homelab folder. `~` also points somewhere else depending on the user.
tools.compose-explainer.f.homePath.fix: Keep everything that belongs to a service in its stack folder (for example `/srv/homelab/<service>/data`) and use `./data` in compose.yaml.
tools.compose-explainer.f.dataOutside.wh: When every service keeps its data in `./data`, every stack folder looks the same: compose.yaml, `.env`, `data/`. That makes backups and moves easier.
tools.compose-explainer.f.dataOutside.fi: Stop the stack, move the folder into `./data/…` and update the path. Config files you write yourself can stay next to compose.yaml.
tools.compose-explainer.f.privileged.why: A privileged container has almost all of the server’s privileges and can easily break out of its isolation. That’s as good as root on the server.
tools.compose-explainer.f.privileged.fix: Only use it if the service’s docs really require it. Often a few rights via `cap_add` or a device via `devices` are enough.
tools.compose-explainer.f.hostNetwork.wh: The container shares the server’s network. Every port it opens is open right away, `ports:` is ignored, and it’s no longer separated from other services.
tools.compose-explainer.f.hostNetwork.fi: Only use it when the service needs it (for example to discover devices on your LAN). Otherwise use regular networks and `ports:` or the reverse proxy.
tools.compose-explainer.f.pidHost.why: The container sees every process on the server and, with enough privileges, can interfere with them.
tools.compose-explainer.f.pidHost.fix: Only for monitoring tools that explicitly require it.
tools.compose-explainer.f.capAdd.why: Capabilities are individual root privileges. Each extra one widens what a compromised container can do.
tools.compose-explainer.f.capAdd.fix: Keep only what the service’s docs ask for (such as `NET_ADMIN` for VPN containers).
tools.compose-explainer.f.capAddStrong.w: These capabilities come very close to root on the server. Breaking out of the container gets much easier.
tools.compose-explainer.f.capAddStrong.f: Check whether the service really needs them. If it does, don’t expose it directly to the internet and only use images you trust.
tools.compose-explainer.f.noNewPrivilege: Processes in the container can’t gain extra privileges.
tools.compose-explainer.f.version.why: Current versions of Docker Compose ignore the field and just print a warning.
tools.compose-explainer.f.noImage.why: Compose doesn’t know what to create the container from.
tools.compose-explainer.f.healthcheck.wh: Docker notices when the service hangs, and other services can wait for it via `depends_on`.
tools.password-hash.local: The hash is computed right here in your browser. Your password and hash never leave your device.
tools.password-hash.costHint: 4 to 15. Each step doubles the work. 10 is a good default.
tools.password-hash.name: Name for Traefik
tools.password-hash.nameHint: Router name of your service, e.g. uptime-kuma. The middleware becomes <name>-auth.
tools.password-hash.stale: Input changed. Create the hash again.
tools.password-hash.errPassword: Enter a password or generate one.
tools.password-hash.errName: Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only, e.g. my-app.
tools.password-hash.tooLong: bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes. The rest of the password is ignored.
tools.password-hash.tinyauthText: This line goes into Tinyauth's .env file. Keep the single quotes: without them, Docker Compose treats every $ in the hash as a variable and breaks it.
tools.password-hash.tinyauthMore: Separate multiple users with commas inside the same quotes. If you put the user straight into compose.yaml instead of .env, write every $ as $$.
tools.password-hash.traefikText: Add these labels to the compose.yaml of the service you want to protect. The first line defines the middleware, the second attaches it to the router. In labels, every $ must be written as $$, so the hash looks doubled here. Compose turns it back into a single $ on startup.
tools.password-hash.traefikMore: For more users, append further user:hash pairs separated by commas. Basic auth only shows the browser's login prompt. For a proper login page, use Tinyauth.
tools.password-hash.htpasswdText: Exactly what htpasswd -nB prints. Use it in an htpasswd file (e.g. Traefik's usersFile or Nginx), without quotes and without doubled $.
tools.password-hash.formatNote: The hash uses the $2y$ prefix, just like htpasswd. Tinyauth and Traefik also accept $2a$ and $2b$, it's the same algorithm.
tools.password-hash.guideLink: Guide: Put Tinyauth in front of your services
tools.proxy-config.idHint: kebab-case, e.g. my-app. Used as the router name.
tools.proxy-config.containerHint: Leave empty to use the ID. Must match container_name or the service name.
tools.proxy-config.portHint: The port the app listens on inside the container (right side of ports:).
tools.proxy-config.subHint: Leave empty to use the ID. In path mode it becomes /<name>.
tools.proxy-config.httpsHint: The service itself only speaks HTTPS, e.g. with its own certificate.
tools.proxy-config.tinyauthHint: Tinyauth asks for a login before every visit.
tools.proxy-config.websocketsHint: For live updates, terminals and chat in the web UI.
tools.proxy-config.leadTraefik: Add these parts to your service's compose.yaml. Traefik reads the labels when the container starts.
tools.proxy-config.leadCaddy: Add this block to your Caddyfile.
tools.proxy-config.leadNpm: In Nginx Proxy Manager, go to Hosts → Proxy Hosts and add a new entry with these values.
tools.proxy-config.leadNet: For the proxy to reach the container, put the service on this network (compose.yaml):
tools.proxy-config.errId: Lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens only, e.g. my-app.
tools.proxy-config.errContainer: Letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens.
tools.proxy-config.errSub: Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, not at the start or end.
tools.proxy-config.noteNoProxy: Your setup has no reverse proxy selected, so this shows Traefik. You can switch above.
tools.proxy-config.notePath: In path mode, the app itself must be able to run under `{path}`. Many apps have a setting like "base URL" or "root path" for this. If yours doesn't, use a subdomain instead.
tools.proxy-config.noteWsAuto: {proxy} passes WebSockets through automatically. Nothing extra needed.
tools.proxy-config.noteTraefikHttps: If the service uses a self-signed certificate, Traefik rejects it. In that case, add `--serversTransport.insecureSkipVerify=true` under `command` in Traefik's compose.yaml. It applies to all services.
tools.proxy-config.noteTraefikAuth: The `tinyauth` middleware is defined by a label on the Tinyauth container, see the [Tinyauth guide](guide). If Tinyauth isn't running, Traefik returns an error.
tools.proxy-config.noteCaddyHttps: You only need `tls_insecure_skip_verify` for a self-signed certificate. If the service has a valid certificate, drop the `transport` block.
tools.proxy-config.noteCaddyAuth: `forward_auth` asks Tinyauth at `/api/auth/caddy` whether you're logged in. Tinyauth has to run on the `{network}` network. Details are in the [Tinyauth docs](tinyauthDocs).
tools.proxy-config.noteCaddyPath: If your Caddyfile already has a block for `{domain}`, only add the `handle_path` part inside it.
tools.proxy-config.noteCaddyReload: Then reload Caddy: `cd {root}/caddy && docker compose exec caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile`
tools.proxy-config.noteNpmHttps: NPM doesn't verify the service's certificate, so self-signed certificates work too.
tools.proxy-config.noteNpmAuth: NPM has no switch for Tinyauth. Paste the `auth_request` block from the [Tinyauth NPM docs](tinyauthNpm) into the Advanced tab.
tools.proxy-config.noteNpmPath: If a proxy host for `{domain}` already exists, edit it and only add the custom location.
tools.proxy-config.checkNet: The `{container}` container is on the `{network}` network, just like the proxy.
tools.proxy-config.checkPorts: No `ports:` needed: the proxy reaches the service internally on port `{port}`. Remove any old port mapping, otherwise the service can be reached around the proxy.
tools.proxy-config.checkDnsSub: A DNS record for `{host}` points to your server, or there is a wildcard record `*.{domain}`.
tools.proxy-config.checkDnsPath: A DNS record for `{domain}` points to your server.
tools.proxy-config.checkTinyauth: Tinyauth is running and also on the `{network}` network ([guide](guide)).
tools.proxy-config.checkStart: Restart the service with `docker compose up -d` and open `{url}`.
tools.proxy-config.checkStartCaddy: Start the service with `docker compose up -d`, reload Caddy and open `{url}`.
tools.proxy-config.checkStartNpm: Start the service with `docker compose up -d`, save the proxy host and open `{url}`.
tools.proxy-config.npmCertNew: Request a new SSL Certificate (Let's Encrypt)
tools.assistant.resultTitle: Here is how we would start in your shoes
tools.assistant.resultLead: This is a suggestion, not a rule. All guides stay available, and you can take a different path at any time.
tools.assistant.applied: Done. Commands and files on this site now match your choices.
tools.assistant.orderLead: The guides that matter most for you, in a sensible order. You can do optional steps later or skip them.
tools.assistant.orderAll: You can still find every other guide in the Setup section.
tools.assistant.q.hardware.hint: Almost anything a few years old is fine to start with.
tools.assistant.q.location.hint: A rented server (VPS) sits in a data center and has a fixed public IP.
tools.assistant.q.ipv4: Does your internet connection have a public IPv4 address?
tools.assistant.q.ipv4.hint: Many fiber, cable and mobile connections don’t have their own (CGNAT or DS-Lite). Classic port forwarding won’t work then.
tools.assistant.q.remote: Should your services be reachable when you’re away from home?
tools.assistant.q.remote.hint: The more people use them, the more login protection and easy access matter.
tools.assistant.q.remote.lan: No, only on my home network
tools.assistant.q.remote.family: Yes, for family and friends too
tools.assistant.q.remote.public: Yes, publicly (e.g. a website, shared links)
tools.assistant.q.style: How do you prefer to work?
tools.assistant.q.style.hint: Both are fine. This is only about which tools suit you better.
tools.assistant.q.learn: How much do you want to learn along the way?
tools.assistant.q.learn.hint: Getting results fast is perfectly fine. Understanding pays off when something breaks.
tools.assistant.q.learn.understand: I want to understand what’s going on
tools.assistant.q.vms: Do you want to try out several systems or VMs?
tools.assistant.q.vms.hint: For example Home Assistant OS, a test Linux or Windows next to your containers.
tools.assistant.q.domain: Do you have your own domain or plan to get one?
tools.assistant.q.domain.hint: A domain usually costs just a few dollars a year and makes HTTPS certificates and nice addresses easy.
tools.assistant.r.platform.proxmox: Proxmox VE with a Docker VM
tools.assistant.why.platform.bare: A lean Debian or Ubuntu Server right on the hardware is the easiest way in: few layers, full performance, and every guide on this site fits one to one.
tools.assistant.why.platform.proxmox: You want to try several systems. Proxmox VE makes that easy: Docker runs in its own VM, and next to it you can create more VMs, take snapshots and simply delete failed experiments.
tools.assistant.why.platform.oldpcRam: Keep an eye on memory with an old PC: with less than 8 GB of RAM, several VMs get tight quickly.
tools.assistant.why.platform.nas: Your NAS can usually run containers directly. That saves a second device and power. The guides still apply; the NAS just handles the operating system, firewall and updates itself.
tools.assistant.why.platform.nasVms: A NAS is usually too weak for many VMs. If that appeals to you, plan a mini PC with Proxmox later on.
tools.assistant.why.platform.vps: On a rented server you install Debian or Ubuntu and set it up just like a server at home. Upside: a fixed IP and always online. Downside: ongoing costs, and your data lives with a provider.
tools.assistant.why.platform.buy: No hardware yet? A used mini PC is the best start for most people: quiet, efficient and powerful enough for lots of services.
tools.assistant.why.platform.both: Combining both is called hybrid: data and heavy services at home, the rented server as the public entrance.
tools.assistant.why.proxy.traefik: You want to understand what’s going on. Traefik asks a bit more at first (labels, routers, middlewares) but gives you the most automation: the config lives in each service’s compose.yaml, and certificates just happen. The guides here use it by default.
tools.assistant.why.proxy.npm: You want fast results and like web interfaces. In Nginx Proxy Manager you add proxy hosts with a click and get certificates with a checkbox. The trade-off: it’s harder to automate.
tools.assistant.why.proxy.caddy: You like files but want to get there fast. Caddy needs just one short, readable text file (the Caddyfile) and handles HTTPS automatically.
tools.assistant.why.proxy.none: Without your own domain and without access for others, you don’t need a reverse proxy at first. You open services by IP and port. You can add a proxy at any time.
tools.assistant.why.access.lan: As long as you only use your services at home, nothing is reachable from the internet. That’s the safest option. You can add a VPN later.
tools.assistant.why.access.vpn: Only you need access, and your line has a public IPv4: your own WireGuard VPN is ideal. Only a single UDP port is open to the outside, and all services stay private.
tools.assistant.why.access.tailscaleCgna: Without a (confirmed) public IPv4, nobody can reach your line directly from outside. Tailscale still connects you, with no port forwarding at all. If you don’t want a third-party coordination server, use Headscale.
tools.assistant.why.access.tailscaleFami: For family and friends, Tailscale is the most convenient: install the app, sign in, done. Your services still stay private. If you don’t want a third-party coordination server, use Headscale.
tools.assistant.why.access.portforward: You have a public IPv4 and want to offer services publicly. Forward only ports 80 and 443 to the reverse proxy in your router, never individual services directly.
tools.assistant.why.access.tunnel: Without a public IPv4, port forwarding won’t work. A tunnel connects from the inside out, so your router stays closed. An alternative without Cloudflare: a small VPS as the entrance, connected to home via WireGuard.
tools.assistant.why.access.vps: The rented server has a fixed public IP. Open only 80 and 443 for the reverse proxy there; admin access goes through SSH or a VPN.
tools.assistant.why.access.vpsBoth: The rented server is your public entrance: it accepts requests on 80/443 and forwards them to your home over a WireGuard VPN. That way you don’t open anything at home, and it even works behind CGNAT.
tools.assistant.why.access.checkIpv4: Check first whether you have a public IPv4. The CGNAT article shows you how.
tools.assistant.why.access.publicProtect: Public means the whole internet comes knocking. Put login protection (Tinyauth or Pocket ID) in front of services without their own login, and keep everything up to date.
tools.assistant.why.url.sub: With your own domain, subdomains like vault.your-domain are the cleanest: every service gets its own address, and every service works with them. One wildcard DNS record covers them all.
tools.assistant.why.url.path: Without your own domain you often have just one hostname (e.g. from a dynamic DNS service). Then the proxy separates services by path. Some services only work with a subdomain, though, so a cheap domain is worth it.
tools.assistant.why.url.noProxy: Without a reverse proxy you open services as http://IP:port. We leave the setting on subdomains so it fits once you add a proxy.
tools.assistant.why.data.stack: Keep everything that belongs to a service in one folder: compose.yaml, .env and data. It’s easy to follow, and one backup of /srv/homelab covers everything.
tools.assistant.why.data.central: On a NAS, data is best kept on the large storage pool, with the configuration separate. That way you can back up and share the data with the NAS’s built-in tools.
tools.assistant.note.proxmoxFirst: Install Proxmox first, then create a VM with Debian or Ubuntu Server. All further guides happen inside that VM.
tools.assistant.note.nasOs: Usually not needed: the NAS comes with its own system.
tools.assistant.note.vpsOs: With most providers you just pick the image with a click.
tools.assistant.note.vpsIp: A rented server already has a fixed IP.
tools.assistant.note.nasFirewall: Many NAS systems have their own firewall in the web interface.
tools.assistant.note.nasDocker: On a NAS you usually install Docker as an app from the package center.
tools.assistant.note.needDomain: Public services need a name that points to you, ideally your own domain.
tools.assistant.note.caddy: There is no dedicated Caddy guide yet. The service page shows you the compose file and Caddyfile.
tools.assistant.note.tailscale: Set up Tailscale using the official instructions. The article explains the differences.
tools.assistant.note.vpsLink: Connects the rented server to your home.
tools.assistant.note.portforward: Forward only 80 and 443 to the reverse proxy.
tools.assistant.note.later: If you want access from outside later on.
tools.security-check.light.none: Answer the questions to get a score.
tools.security-check.light.red: Quite a bit left to do
tools.security-check.nextEmpty: Nothing urgent left. Go through the list again from time to time.
tools.security-check.note: “Don’t know” counts as “no”. Critical items count three times, important ones twice. This is a rough estimate, not a security audit.
tools.security-check.i.ssh-keys: SSH login only with a key, password login is off
tools.security-check.h.ssh-keys: Passwords can be guessed, keys practically can’t. Bots try passwords around the clock.
tools.security-check.i.root-login: Root can’t log in over SSH
tools.security-check.h.root-login: Root is the first username every attacker tries. Work with your own user and sudo.
tools.security-check.i.sudo-user: You work with your own user and sudo
tools.security-check.h.sudo-user: That way every admin command leaves a trace, and mistakes as root happen less often.
tools.security-check.h.ufw: Block all incoming traffic by default and only allow what you really need.
tools.security-check.i.open-ports: Only 80/443 or the VPN port are open from outside
tools.security-check.h.open-ports: Every extra open port is another door. Check the port forwards on your router and the open ports on your server.
tools.security-check.h.admin-uis: Portainer, the Traefik dashboard or NPM on port 81 belong on your home network or behind the VPN.
tools.security-check.i.docker-ports: Container ports bind only to 127.0.0.1 or sit behind the proxy
tools.security-check.h.docker-ports: Docker opens published ports past the firewall. Without ports:, or with 127.0.0.1:, a service is only reachable through the proxy.
tools.security-check.h.docker-sock: Whoever controls the Docker socket has root on the server. Only trusted containers get it, ideally read-only or through a socket proxy.
tools.security-check.i.secrets: Secrets live in .env with chmod 600 and not in Git
tools.security-check.h.secrets: Passwords don’t belong in compose.yaml and never in a public repository.
tools.security-check.i.login-protection: Services without their own login are protected (SSO, Tinyauth or similar)
tools.security-check.h.login-protection: Some services have no login or only a weak one. A login layer in front closes that gap.
tools.security-check.i.crowdsec: CrowdSec or similar blocks suspicious IPs
tools.security-check.h.crowdsec: Spots brute force and scans in your logs and blocks known attackers. Most useful for public services.
tools.security-check.h.auto-updates: Unattended upgrades installs security updates without you having to remember.
tools.security-check.i.image-tags: Images use pinned tags and you have an update routine
tools.security-check.h.image-tags: With pinned tags you know what’s running. A routine (e.g. Renovate or a fixed date) makes sure you still stay current.
tools.security-check.h.backup-auto: A backup you have to remember is missing exactly when you need it.
tools.security-check.i.backup-offsite: One copy is stored off-site (3-2-1 rule)
tools.security-check.h.backup-offsite: Three copies, two media, one off-site. Otherwise fire, theft or ransomware hit your server and backup at the same time.
tools.security-check.h.restore-tested: Only a successful restore proves your backup works.
tools.security-check.i.monitoring: Monitoring alerts you to outages and full disks
tools.security-check.h.monitoring: Notifications by email or app, before someone asks you why nothing works.
tools.security-check.i.emergency-plan: There’s an emergency plan and documentation
tools.security-check.h.emergency-plan: Where are the backups and keys, and who can help in an emergency? Write it down while everything still works.
tools.power-calculator.loadHint: A homelab idles most of the time. 10% load is realistic for most setups.
tools.power-calculator.priceAssumption: Assumption: 0.35 per kWh (a rough average in Germany). Enter the price from your own power bill.
tools.power-calculator.avg: Average power of all devices: {w} W
tools.power-calculator.perWatt: Rule of thumb: 1 W of constant load costs you about {cost} a year.
tools.power-calculator.compareHint: One device, idle, at your price and runtime.
tools.borgmatic.src.title: What to back up
tools.borgmatic.src.lead: Your homelab folder from “My setup” is always included. In “central” mode, the data folder is added too, unless it already sits inside it.
tools.borgmatic.src.extraHint: For example, a media library on a second disk that you mounted into a stack.
tools.borgmatic.src.excludeCaches: Skip cache folders marked with CACHEDIR.TAG
tools.borgmatic.src.excludesHint: Borg patterns: * matches any characters, across folder boundaries too.
tools.borgmatic.src.immich: Immich: files that can be regenerated
tools.borgmatic.repo.title: Backup targets
tools.borgmatic.repo.lead: You can add several targets, for example a USB disk and a machine offsite. borgmatic backs up to each one in turn.
tools.borgmatic.repo.label: Name (label)
tools.borgmatic.repo.localHint: The disk has to be mounted permanently, for example via /etc/fstab.
tools.borgmatic.repo.sshHint: Borg must be installed on the target machine, and root must be able to log in with an SSH key. ./borg means the folder borg in the user's home directory.
tools.borgmatic.repo.urlHint: For example BorgBase, Hetzner Storage Box or rsync.net. You'll find the SSH address in the provider's web interface.
tools.borgmatic.enc.title: Encryption and compression
tools.borgmatic.enc.keyHint: Keep the passphrase and the exported key (borgmatic key export) in your password manager. Without both, your backups are worthless.
tools.borgmatic.enc.archiveNameHint: Leave empty for the default: host name plus date and time.
tools.borgmatic.keep.title: Retention and checks
tools.borgmatic.keep.lead: How many archives borgmatic keeps. 0 means: don't use this level.
tools.borgmatic.db.title: Databases
tools.borgmatic.db.lead: Services with a database from your selection. For each one, pick how the database gets into a clean state before the backup.
tools.borgmatic.db.more: The selection is shared by all tools. borgmatic backs up services without a database as plain files.
tools.borgmatic.modeHint.sqlite: “Copy with sqlite3” needs the sqlite3 package on the server.
tools.borgmatic.modeHint.stop: Stopped stacks are offline during the backup. They start again afterwards, even if the backup fails.
tools.borgmatic.modeHint.none: “Files only” can catch a database while it's writing. The copy may then be unusable.
tools.borgmatic.notify.title: Notifications
tools.borgmatic.notify.lead: So you notice when a backup fails or doesn't run at all.
tools.borgmatic.notify.kumaHint: Leave empty for status.<your domain>. The generator drops everything from the question mark on, borgmatic adds that part itself.
tools.borgmatic.steps.title: Next steps
tools.borgmatic.steps.passphrase: Create the passphrase if you haven't yet. Then copy it into your password manager (sudo cat shows it).
tools.borgmatic.steps.sqlite: Install sqlite3 so the SQLite copies work:
tools.borgmatic.steps.install: Copy config.yaml to the server (with scp, for example), store it readable for root only and check it:
tools.borgmatic.steps.init: Create the repository once and export the key. The output of key export goes into your password manager, next to the passphrase:
tools.borgmatic.steps.test: Run a first backup as a test. Then set up the nightly timer as described in the guide:
tools.borgmatic.modeHint.stopNotify: You're stopping a stack that notifications go through (Uptime Kuma, ntfy or the reverse proxy). The success ping may then get lost because it's still starting up. Use “Copy with sqlite3” for it instead.
table.label: Table, scrolls sideways
tools.password-hash.hashLead: For logins that shouldn't store a plain-text password: Tinyauth, Traefik basic auth or an htpasswd file.
tools.secret.title: Generate a secret
tools.secret.lead: Random values for tokens, keys and database passwords in your .env. Pick a length and the characters; the value comes from your browser's random number generator.
tools.secret.setHint.hex: Works everywhere. Same format as openssl rand -hex. Good for secrets that need a fixed length in hex.
tools.secret.setHint.alnum: Works everywhere, more randomness per character. Good for passwords and tokens.
tools.secret.setHint.base64url: Letters, digits, - and _. Compact and safe in URLs.
